title: Design an Experimentation / A-B Testing Platform
prompt: Design an experimentation platform that lets teams run A/B tests and feature rollouts across a large product. It must assign users to variants deterministically, expose assignments at low latency, compute experiment metrics, and run a statistics engine that reports significance and guardrails. Assume thousands of concurrent experiments and a very large user base.
blurb: The platform behind trustworthy A/B tests: deterministic assignment, a metrics pipeline, and a stats engine that resists peeking and interference.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (assignment, targeting, metrics, stats reports, guardrails, ramp/rollback) from non-functional (low-latency assignment, correctness/trustworthiness, isolation between experiments, auditability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about number of concurrent experiments, user base size, unit of randomization, metric types, real-time vs batch results, org guardrails.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives assignment QPS, config size, exposure-event volume, metrics-pipeline throughput, storage for events and results.

rubric.label: Deterministic assignment
rubric.description: Hash(user_id, experiment_salt) → bucket; sticky, uniform, independent across experiments; low-latency edge/SDK evaluation; mutual exclusion / layers for overlapping experiments.

rubric.label: Metrics pipeline
rubric.description: Exposure logging, event ingestion, joining exposures to metric events, batch + streaming aggregation, metric definitions/registry, data-quality checks.

rubric.label: Statistics engine
rubric.description: Hypothesis testing, variance reduction (CUPED), sequential/peeking correction, multiple comparisons, ratio metrics (delta method), minimum detectable effect / power.

rubric.label: Experiment integrity & interference
rubric.description: SRM (sample-ratio mismatch) detection, network/interference effects, novelty effects, carryover, guardrail metrics, isolation between experiments.

rubric.label: Result validity & monitoring (evaluation)
rubric.description: Detecting invalid experiments (SRM, logging bugs, drift in traffic mix), pre-experiment A/A tests, monitoring metric health and pipeline correctness over time.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Config service → assignment SDK/edge → exposure + event logging → metrics pipeline → stats engine → results UI; ramp/rollback controls and guardrails.

rubric.label: Scaling & reliability
rubric.description: Config distribution at scale, low-latency assignment with local evaluation, high-throughput event pipeline, incremental/streaming metric computation, availability with safe defaults.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Assignment latency, exposure/event volumes, pipeline lag, SRM/guardrail alerts, config propagation lag, result freshness.

rubric.label: Governance & trust
rubric.description: Access control on experiment config, audit trail, preventing p-hacking/peeking abuse, guardrail enforcement, privacy of user-level data.

functional_requirements: Assign users to variants deterministically and stickily
Target experiments by attributes/segments and ramp exposure
Log exposures and collect metric events
Compute metrics per variant and run a statistics engine
Report significance, confidence intervals, and guardrails
Support safe ramp-up and instant rollback
nonfunctional_requirements: Assignment evaluated at very low latency (ideally local/edge)
Trustworthy results — correctness over speed; detect invalid experiments
Isolation: overlapping experiments must not confound each other
Scale to thousands of concurrent experiments and huge traffic
Auditable config changes and reproducible analyses
clarifying_questions: How many concurrent experiments and how large is the user base?
Unit of randomization — user, session, device, account, cluster?
Metric types — means, proportions, ratios, per-user aggregates?
Do teams need near-real-time readouts or is daily batch fine?
What org-wide guardrail metrics must every experiment respect?
Do experiments overlap, requiring mutual exclusion / layering?
qualifying_questions: Client-side (SDK/edge) or server-side assignment, or both?
Are there network/marketplace interference effects (two-sided platform)?
Any need for switchback or cluster-randomized designs?

estimations.assignment_qps: If assignment is evaluated per request, effectively product traffic QPS (100Ks-Ms/s) — must be local, not a network call
estimations.config: Thousands of experiments × targeting rules → MBs of config, pushed to SDKs/edge and cached
estimations.exposure_events: One exposure log per user-experiment first-touch + metric events → tens of billions/day
estimations.metrics_pipeline: High-throughput stream + daily batch; storage for raw events (PBs over time) + aggregated results
estimations.results: Per experiment × variant × metric × day aggregates — modest, but many experiments

data_model: experiments(exp_id PK, hypothesis, layer, variants[], targeting, allocation, status, owner)
assignments(logged lazily): exposure(user_id, exp_id, variant, ts, context)
results(exp_id, variant, metric_id, date, estimate, ci, p_value, n)
api_design: getVariant(user_id, exp_id) → variant  (evaluated locally via cached config + hash; logs exposure)
GET /v1/experiments/{id}/results → { per-variant metrics, ci, p_value, srm_status, guardrails }
reference.high_level_design: A config service holds experiment definitions (variants, targeting, allocation, layer) and pushes them to SDKs/edge evaluators. Assignment is a pure function: hash(user_id, experiment_salt) → bucket → variant, evaluated locally so there's no network hop, and it's sticky and independent across experiments; overlapping experiments are organized into mutually-exclusive layers so they don't confound. The first exposure per user-experiment is logged. Metric events stream into an ingestion layer; a metrics pipeline (streaming for early reads, batch for authoritative daily results) joins exposures to events, applies metric definitions, and produces per-variant aggregates. A statistics engine computes estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values with variance reduction (CUPED), sequential-testing correction to allow safe peeking, multiple-comparison control, and the delta method for ratio metrics. An integrity monitor runs SRM checks and guardrail evaluation, flagging invalid experiments. Results surface in a UI with ramp/rollback controls, all config changes audited.

deep_dives.probe: Design deterministic assignment. Why hash(user_id, per-experiment salt)? How do you keep it sticky, uniform, and independent across experiments, and evaluate it at request latency?
Two experiments touch the same surface. How do you prevent them from confounding — mutual exclusion, layers/universes, orthogonal randomization?

Teams stare at dashboards and stop when it's 'significant.' Why is naive peeking wrong, and how does your stats engine allow continuous monitoring — sequential tests / always-valid p-values / Bayesian?
How do you increase sensitivity without more traffic — CUPED / covariate adjustment? What's the intuition and what does it require?
You expected 50/50 but see 50.8/49.2 over millions of users. Why does that invalidate the experiment, how do you detect it, and what causes it?
A metric like clicks-per-session is a ratio of sums where the denominator varies per user. Why can't you use a naive t-test, and how does the delta method fix the variance?

Experiment config changes (ramp, targeting, kill-switch) in the config service. How does that change propagate to every SDK/edge evaluator quickly and consistently, so you don't have users on stale allocations?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions config or targeting or flag
followup_bank.question: When an experiment's config changes (ramp, kill-switch, targeting) in the source config store, how does that propagate to all SDK/edge evaluators — change-stream/push vs polling? What's your propagation-lag bound and consistency story?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cache or SDK or edge
followup_bank.question: SDKs cache experiment config locally. What's the refresh/eviction policy, and when config changes how do you invalidate stale-after-change cached config so users aren't stuck on old allocations?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions significance or p-value or stop
followup_bank.question: How do you prevent invalid conclusions from peeking — sequential testing, always-valid p-values, or a fixed-horizon design with power analysis?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions assignment or hash or bucket
followup_bank.question: How do you guarantee assignment is sticky, uniform, and independent across overlapping experiments?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions SRM or sample ratio or imbalance
followup_bank.question: What's your SRM detection threshold and what are the common root causes you'd investigate?
For a ratio metric where the denominator varies per user, how do you compute correct variance — delta method / bootstrap?

scaling: Local/edge assignment via cached config — no per-request network call
Push config updates via a fast propagation channel with versioning
Horizontally scaled event ingestion; partition by user/experiment
Streaming for early reads + batch for authoritative results
Incremental/materialized aggregation to avoid full recompute
bottlenecks: Config propagation lag causing inconsistent assignment
Exposure/event volume in the metrics pipeline
Join of exposures to metric events at scale
Stats compute across many experiments × metrics × slices
tradeoffs: Local assignment (fast, config-lag risk) vs server assignment (consistent, latency)
Streaming results (fast, noisier) vs batch (authoritative, delayed)
Sequential tests (safe peeking, less power) vs fixed-horizon (more power, no peeking)
More slices/metrics (insight) vs multiple-comparison + compute cost
Sensitivity via CUPED (complex) vs more traffic/longer runs
alternative_solutions: Bayesian A/B framework with posteriors instead of frequentist p-values
Switchback / cluster randomization for marketplace interference
Server-side-only assignment for strong consistency at latency cost
observability: SRM and guardrail alerts per experiment
A/A test health checks and metric-definition drift
Result freshness and stats-engine job status
security: RBAC + approval workflow on experiment config; full audit trail
Guardrail enforcement and auto-rollback on regressions
Discourage p-hacking (fixed metrics/hypothesis registered up front)
Privacy of user-level exposure/event data; aggregation for reporting
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer makes assignment a deterministic, local pure function — hash(user_id, per-experiment salt) → bucket — that's sticky, uniform, and independent across experiments, with overlapping experiments organized into mutually-exclusive layers, so it evaluates at request latency without a network hop. It logs exposures and builds a metrics pipeline (streaming for early reads, batch for authoritative results) that joins exposures to events under a governed metric registry with data-quality checks. Its statistics engine is the differentiator: variance reduction (CUPED), sequential/always-valid tests so teams can peek safely, multiple-comparison control, and the delta method for ratio metrics — plus SRM detection and guardrail monitoring to catch invalid experiments. It treats config propagation as a correctness concern (fast, versioned updates so no one is stuck on stale allocations), enforces governance/audit, and monitors pipeline and result health continuously. The theme is trustworthiness: correct assignment, correct statistics, and detection of the many ways experiments silently go wrong.

interviewer_notes: This platform lives or dies on trustworthiness, so reward candidates who prioritize correctness over cleverness. Assignment should be a deterministic, locally-evaluated hash — if they propose a network call per assignment, probe latency and push them to edge/SDK evaluation, then ask how overlapping experiments avoid confounding (layers). The senior separator is the statistics engine: make them address peeking (why naive significance-chasing is wrong; sequential/always-valid tests), ratio-metric variance (delta method), variance reduction (CUPED), and SRM as an experiment-invalidation signal. A candidate who only says 't-test for significance' is mid-level. Treat SRM/guardrails/A-A tests as the 'evaluation/validity' dimension — detecting when an experiment is silently broken. When they mention the config store, hit the CDC/propagation-freshness probe: how config changes reach every evaluator fast and consistently. When they mention SDK/edge config caching, probe refresh/eviction and stale-after-change. Reserve time for the metrics pipeline (exposure-to-event joins, late/duplicate events) and governance/audit. Weak candidates build a bucketing service; strong ones build a trustworthy inference system with integrity checks.
